answer:
Record the treatment as one instance of E11 Modification per repair campaign (or one per cabinet if the six were worked on separately), with P31 has modified pointing at each cabinet. E11 is the right class without any stretching: its 7.3.2 scope note says in so many words that "It also includes the conservation treatment of an object."

On the actual question — yes, more than one person should be linked, and the CRM expects that. P14 carried out by is quantified "many to many, necessary (1,n:0,n)": an activity must have at least one actor and may have any number. So recording several people is the normal case, not a workaround for an awkward fact. What distinguishes them is P14.1 in the role of (range E55 Type), whose whole job is to specify the nature of each actor's participation; the CRM's own P14 example uses it to say Michelangelo was there "in the role of master craftsman", which is exactly the master/executant distinction this case turns on.

Concretely:

1. The two apprentices — P14 carried out by, each as a separate E21 Person, P14.1 in the role of a term such as 'conservation technician' or 'executant'. They performed the filling, regluing and touch-up. Active participation, causally responsible for the physical change, no argument.

2. The studio principal — also P14 carried out by, P14.1 in the role of 'supervising conservator' (or 'master conservator'). The decisive words in the scope note are "It implies causal or legal responsibility" — the disjunction. She did not touch the cabinets, but she directed the work and approved it, so she is causally responsible for it and, as the studio's principal, legally answerable for it. Nothing in P14 requires the actor's own hands on the object. If you record only her (as the invoice does), you lose the executants; if you record only the apprentices, you lose the person answerable for the result. Record all three of these, differentiated by role.

3. The museum's conservation officer — do NOT link her with P14. She neither performed the work nor shared responsibility for it; she inspected it on the museum's behalf. This exact boundary was argued in thread t1546, where Martin Doerr states that "P14 is meant in an active sense" and that necessary-but-passive presence is not what "causal" meant, illustrating it with "patients in a surgery are necessary, but do not carry it out". In the same thread Athanasios Velios proposed adding to the scope note that where actors "are active without sharing the responsibility of the activity", P11 had participant should be used instead. (Caveat, verified: that addition did not make it into the published 7.3.2 text, which still reads only "This property describes the active participation... It implies causal or legal responsibility." So this is the SIG's stated reading rather than published wording.) Two ways to place her, and I would do both:
   - P11 had participant on the E11 Modification, if all you want on record is that she was there while it happened. P11 "does not imply any causal relationship", which is precisely the claim you want to avoid making.
   - Better, because it says what she actually did: model each of her two visits as its own E14 Condition Assessment, P14 carried out by her, P34 concerned the cabinets. E14's scope note says the assessment "may be carried out by inspection", and its published examples are named conservators inspecting objects. That way she is the actor of her own activity rather than a diluted actor of someone else's.

An alternative to relying on P14.1, if you need master and executant kept structurally apart rather than distinguished by a role term: partition the event. One outer E11 Modification carried out by the principal (and/or the workshop), P9 consists of component activities each carried out by one apprentice. This is the pattern the SIG reached for in t1345 when the same problem arose as 'acting on behalf of another' — Robert Sanderson: "the event partitioning pattern is not so unreasonable". I would not do it here: it is only worth the extra nodes if you know which apprentice performed which operation, and the case says you do not. Use P14.1 roles.

One thing the case invites that is not among the three people: the invoice is issued by the workshop, not by the principal personally. If you want the legally responsible party on record, add the workshop as an E74 Group with its own P14 carried out by. Thread t1477 shows the SIG treating exactly this 'workshop of / studio of' group attribution as an unsettled question — no refinement of P14 for groups was agreed — so it stays a plain P14 to a Group, meaning 'carried out by one or more members in the name of the group'. This is also, per SIG issue 488 (closed pending CRMsoc), the outstanding gap: the CRM has no agreed way to say 'X acted as representative of Y'.

Finally, a caution about evidence rather than classes. The only source for the principal's supervision is the workshop's own invoice. If the museum needs to keep the workshop's claim distinct from its own knowledge, the CRM's recommended practice (Modelling principles > Authorship of Knowledge Base Contents) is to wrap the assertion in an E13 Attribute Assignment attributed to the workshop, rather than asserting P14 flatly. I have not proposed that here because the question asked which links to make, not how to source them, but the distinction matters if the invoice is ever disputed.

rejected_alternatives.option: P11 had participant for the apprentices and the principal
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Its scope note says it "does not imply any causal relationship". That understates both the apprentices, who caused the physical change, and the principal, who bears legal responsibility for it. P11 is the right level only for the museum's officer.

rejected_alternatives.option: P12 occurred in the presence of for the museum's conservation officer
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Too weak, and the wrong level. P12 is the superproperty for mere presence with range E77 Persistent Item; she was an Actor doing something deliberate (inspecting). P11 had participant is the correct rung, and an E14 Condition Assessment of her own is better still.

rejected_alternatives.option: Recording only the studio principal, as the invoice does
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Nothing forces a single actor. P14's quantification is (1,n:0,n) — at least one, any number. Collapsing the work onto the supervisor discards the fact that two apprentices performed it, which the museum evidently knows.

E12 is a subclass of E11 restricted to activities that bring a new item into existence. The six cabinets already existed and kept their identities; nothing was produced. E11 Modification is the correct level, and its scope note names conservation treatment explicitly.

rejected_alternatives.option: E79 Part Addition for the filling and regluing
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Also an E11 subclass, and arguably applicable, but it changes nothing about the actor question and mis-describes the work: P111 added ranges over E18 Physical Thing, i.e. an added part with its own identity, whereas fill material and adhesive are material, which E11 already carries via P126 employed. Not worth the extra nodes here.

rejected_alternatives.option: E13 Attribute Assignment for the officer's site visits
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E14 Condition Assessment is its subclass and fits better: she was assessing the state of specific objects, which is what E14 is for and what P34 concerned links. Plain E13 would be right only if she were assigning some property other than condition.

siblings_considered.why_not: E87 Curation Activity covers activities managing and preserving an E78 Curated Holding under a curation plan — a collection-level, policy-driven activity. It does not record a physical change to a specific object and does not carry P31 has modified. The repair physically altered six named cabinets, which is E11's definition.

For the three individuals, E74 Group is wrong: they are identified natural persons, and their individually differing responsibility is the very thing the question asks about. Collapsing them into a collective actor would erase the distinction. (E74 is proposed separately, for the workshop as a firm.)

For the workshop, E21 Person is wrong: the invoice is issued by the studio as an organisation, and its legal answerability is not reducible to the principal as a private individual — even though she is also recorded, in her own right, under P14.

A role term such as 'supervising conservator' is a concept from a controlled vocabulary used to classify a participation, not a set of propositions about the world, which is what E89 Propositional Object comprises. P14.1 in the role of also declares E55 Type as its range outright.

E16 Measurement requires a systematic objective procedure yielding a value, and hangs an E54 Dimension off the result. The officer looked at progress on two visits; nothing was measured. E14 explicitly allows assessment "by inspection".

notes: Three friction points. (1) The published 7.3.2 P14 scope note is only two sentences long and does not resolve this case on its own — 'causal or legal responsibility' is all you get. The reasoning that settles it (active sense; necessary-but-passive participation goes to P11) lives in thread t1546 and was never folded into the text, so a reader consulting only the specification would be left guessing. I checked for the folded-in wording with docs and it is not there. (2) `quote` needs the document chunk id, and neither `docs` nor `issue` prints one; I had to re-run the docs search with --json to discover the `crm732#P14` form. `issue:488` is not a resolvable source for `quote`, so the E14-Condition-Assessment-with-two-conservators example that appeared in the Issue 488 background preview could not be verified as a quotation and I have described issue 488 only in general terms. (3) I searched the mailing list directly for the conservator/supervisor/apprentice split and found nothing on point; the SIG has argued the boundary abstractly (baptised child, surgical patient, workshop-of attribution) but never this concrete division of labour. For completeness: I grepped my own saved `ontology` tool output to filter the class list, not the corpus. E14 as the home for the officer's visits is the least certain part of this answer — 'checking progress' is not literally 'assessing the state of preservation', so if her visits produced no condition finding, a plain E7 Activity typed as an inspection, plus P11 on the treatment, is the safer record. Note also that a fully-specified E14 carries P35 has identified and P177 assigned property of type as necessary properties, which need an E3 Condition State the case does not supply.
